write.desc: This topic proves the algebraic and order limit theorems for sequences from the epsilon-N definition, including the squeeze theorem, limits of |a_n| and sqrt(a_n), the laws for sequences tending to infinity, and the standard limits that follow from them. These points belong together because they all use the same small set of proof moves: splitting epsilon, adding and subtracting a term, and bounding one factor.

points.name: Constant multiple law
points.what: The learner can prove that if a_n -> L then c*a_n -> cL by running the definition with epsilon/|c|, treat the case c = 0 separately, and see this as the simplest example of choosing the epsilon to feed into a known limit.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Sum and difference law (the epsilon/2 technique)
points.what: The learner can prove that if a_n -> a and b_n -> b then a_n + b_n -> a + b and a_n - b_n -> a - b, by applying each hypothesis with epsilon/2, taking N as the larger of the two thresholds and combining with the triangle inequality. They can reuse this splitting pattern in other proofs.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Null sequences and bounded times null
points.what: The learner knows that a_n -> L exactly when a_n - L -> 0, and that a_n -> 0 exactly when |a_n| -> 0. They can prove that a bounded sequence times a sequence tending to 0 tends to 0, and use this on examples such as sin(n)/n.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Product law
points.what: The learner can prove that a_n b_n -> ab by writing a_n b_n - ab = a_n(b_n - b) + b(a_n - a), bounding |a_n| by a constant M because convergent sequences are bounded, and choosing the two thresholds so that each piece is below epsilon/2. They understand why boundedness is needed and can reproduce and adapt the add-and-subtract step.

points.name: A nonzero limit keeps the sequence away from zero
points.what: The learner can prove that if b_n -> b with b != 0, then from some N on |b_n| > |b|/2, by applying the definition with epsilon = |b|/2 and the reverse triangle inequality. They see why this fails when b = 0.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Reciprocal and quotient law
points.what: The learner can prove that 1/b_n -> 1/b when b_n -> b and b != 0 (with b_n != 0), by bounding |1/b_n - 1/b| = |b - b_n|/(|b_n||b|) using the lower bound on |b_n|. They then obtain a_n/b_n -> a/b from the product law, and know exactly which hypotheses the quotient law needs.

points.name: Using the algebraic limit theorem
points.what: The learner can compute limits such as (3n^2 + 1)/(2n^2 - n) by dividing by the highest power and applying the laws step by step, justifying each step. They know that the laws need the component limits to exist, and can give counterexamples to false converses (for example a_n + b_n can converge while a_n and b_n do not).

points.name: Order limit theorem
points.what: The learner can prove by contradiction that if a_n >= 0 for all large n and a_n -> a then a >= 0, and deduce that a_n <= b_n implies lim a_n <= lim b_n and that c <= a_n <= d implies c <= lim a_n <= d. They know that strict inequalities can become equalities in the limit, as 1/n > 0 with limit 0 shows.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Squeeze theorem
points.what: The learner can prove that if a_n <= x_n <= b_n eventually and a_n, b_n both tend to L, then x_n -> L, directly from the definition (and see why the order limit theorem alone does not give it, since it assumes the limit exists). They can apply it to examples such as sin(n)/n and sqrt(n^2 + 1) - n.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Limit of |a_n|
points.what: The learner can prove that a_n -> a implies |a_n| -> |a| using the reverse triangle inequality, and knows that the converse fails in general (for example (-1)^n) but holds when a = 0.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: Limit of sqrt(a_n)
points.what: The learner can prove that if a_n >= 0 and a_n -> a then sqrt(a_n) -> sqrt(a), handling a = 0 directly from the definition and a > 0 by rationalising: |sqrt(a_n) - sqrt(a)| = |a_n - a|/(sqrt(a_n) + sqrt(a)) <= |a_n - a|/sqrt(a).
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence

points.name: The epsilon/3 technique
points.what: The learner can bound a distance by a chain of three terms with the triangle inequality, |x - z| <= |x - y| + |y - w| + |w - z|, and make each term less than epsilon/3, working through an example such as the limit of a_n + b_n + c_n or of a_n b_n c_n. They recognise this as the general pattern of splitting epsilon into as many pieces as the estimate has, which later proofs (Cauchy criterion, uniform limits) reuse.

points.name: Limit laws for sequences tending to infinity
points.what: The learner can prove that if a_n -> +infinity then a_n + b_n -> +infinity when b_n is bounded below, c*a_n -> +infinity for c > 0, a_n b_n -> +infinity when b_n -> b > 0, and 1/a_n -> 0; and conversely that 1/a_n -> +infinity when a_n -> 0 with a_n > 0. They can use comparison: a_n <= b_n and a_n -> +infinity imply b_n -> +infinity.
outside: definition of divergence to plus or minus infinity (M-N definition)

points.name: Indeterminate forms
points.what: The learner knows why no general law exists for infinity - infinity, 0 * infinity, infinity/infinity and 0/0, and can give pairs of sequences showing that each form can lead to any finite limit, to infinity or to no limit. They can resolve such limits by algebraic rewriting before applying the laws.

points.name: Bernoulli's inequality and r^n for |r| < 1
points.what: The learner can prove Bernoulli's inequality (1 + h)^n >= 1 + nh for h >= -1 by induction, and use it to show r^n -> 0 for |r| < 1 by writing 1/|r| = 1 + h and squeezing |r|^n between 0 and 1/(nh). They can also show that r^n diverges for |r| > 1 and for r = -1.

points.name: c^(1/n) tends to 1
points.what: The learner can prove that c^(1/n) -> 1 for c > 1 by writing c^(1/n) = 1 + h_n and using Bernoulli's inequality to get 0 <= h_n <= (c - 1)/n, then handle 0 < c < 1 with the reciprocal law.

points.name: n^(1/n) tends to 1
points.what: The learner can prove that n^(1/n) -> 1 by writing n^(1/n) = 1 + h_n, keeping only the second term of the binomial expansion to get n >= n(n-1)/2 * h_n^2, so that 0 <= h_n <= sqrt(2/(n-1)), and finishing with the squeeze theorem.

points.name: Polynomial versus exponential growth
points.what: The learner can prove that n/2^n -> 0 and more generally n^k/a^n -> 0 for a > 1 and fixed k, by bounding a^n below with one term of the binomial expansion and squeezing (or by reducing n^k/a^n to the k-th power of n/b^n with b = a^(1/k) and using the product law). They can use this to compare growth rates in limit computations.

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.3, The Algebraic and Order Limit Theorems (with its exercises, including the squeeze theorem and sqrt(x_n))

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 3.1 (Bernoulli examples, c^(1/n), n^(1/n)), Section 3.2 Limit Theorems, Section 3.6 Properly Divergent Sequences

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 3: Theorem 3.3 (algebraic limit laws) and Theorem 3.20 (some special sequences: p^(1/n), n^(1/n), n^a/(1+p)^n, x^n)
